nodes.content: Determine when unpaired RNA and chromatin accessibility measurements support transferable perturbation-response prediction despite donor–batch confounding.
requirements: Reduce perturbation-response RMSE by 15% versus RNA-only models on unseen donors and perturbations.
Characterize identifiability assumptions separating biological coupling from batch effects, including cases where separation is impossible.

nodes.content: Fit batch-aware latent RNA–ATAC alignment via shared cell-state anchors; test donor/perturbation holdouts and flag rank-deficient donor–batch designs.
Which donor–batch incidence patterns make shared-anchor RNA–ATAC coupling identifiable, and when does complete donor nesting make separation impossible?
Under additive batch effects, invariant anchors and crossed donor–batch observations identify RNA–ATAC coupling; nested designs confound donor and batch.
Simulate crossed and nested donor–batch layouts, vary anchor invariance, and quantify coupling identifiability with profile likelihood and held-out RMSE.
Simulate six donors across three crossed or nested batches with 0–20% anchor shifts; measure coupling-profile curvature and holdout RMSE.
With invariant anchors, normalized coupling-profile curvature was 0.42 in crossed designs versus <0.01 in nested designs.
Restrict identifiable-coupling claims to crossed donor–batch designs with invariant anchors; flag nested layouts as nonidentifiable.
DonorBatchSim v1 contains crossed/nested simulations, anchor-shift sweeps, coupling-profile curvature plots, and held-out perturbation RMSE tables.
Using DonorBatchSim v1 replicates, profile RNA–ATAC coupling under 0%, 10%, and 20% anchor drift across crossed and nested layouts.
DonorBatchSim v1: crossed donors, additive batches, and two shared invariant anchors with identical RNA profiles gave coupling-profile curvature <0.01.
Coupling requires crossed donor–batch observations and full-rank, matched cell-state anchors; identical anchors or nested designs preclude separation.
At what anchor rank and donor–batch overlap does unpaired ATAC lower joint donor–perturbation holdout RMSE by ≥15%?
Grid-search DonorBatchSim v1 across anchor ranks 1–4 and 0–3 cross-batch donors; compare RNA–ATAC against RNA-only unseen-donor/perturbation RMSE.
AnchorOverlapGrid v1 reports anchor rank, cross-batch donor overlap, joint donor–perturbation holdout RMSE, and improvement versus RNA-only.
AnchorOverlapGrid v1: rank-3 anchors and three cross-batch donors yielded joint-holdout RNA–ATAC RMSE 0.66 versus RNA-only 0.80 (17.5% lower).
Using AnchorOverlapGrid v1, ablate batch correction across anchor ranks and donor overlaps; compare joint-holdout RMSE against RNA-only.
With rank-3 anchors but one cross-batch donor, batch-corrected RNA–ATAC RMSE was 0.83 versus RNA-only 0.80 on joint holdouts.
Advance RNA–ATAC for rank-3 anchors with three cross-batch donors; one-donor overlap underperforms RNA-only.
Augment RNA-only predictors with ATAC-derived target-to-gene priors, calibrated using cross-batch donor replicates and negative-control peaks.
Can negative-control peaks distinguish transferable target-to-gene links from batch-driven accessibility correlations in unpaired ATAC?
With crossed donors, batch-only control peaks and validated target–peak–gene maps identify target-specific coupling despite rank-deficient shared anchors.
Compare validated target–peak–gene priors with and without batch-only control-peak adjustment across crossed/nested designs, measuring identifiability and joint-holdout RMSE.
In DonorBatchSim v1, ablate control-peak adjustment with known target–peak–gene links and rank-1 anchors; compare crossed/nested curvature and joint-holdout RMSE.
Crossed rank-1 designs with validated links: control-peak adjustment raised target-coupling curvature from <0.01 to 0.29; nested designs remained <0.01.
Stress-test crossed rank-1 designs by corrupting 0–50% of target–peak–gene links; measure coupling curvature and joint-holdout RMSE.
At 0% link corruption, crossed rank-1 donors with batch-exclusive perturbations retained curvature <0.01 despite validated maps and batch-only controls.
In crossed-donor designs, validated links and batch-only controls identify target coupling with rank-1 anchors only when perturbations bridge batches.
With validated maps and crossed rank-1 donors, vary perturbation batch overlap and control-peak adjustment; measure coupling curvature and joint-holdout RMSE.
In crossed rank-1 simulations, compare batch-exclusive versus batch-bridging perturbations with/without control-peak adjustment; measure target-coupling curvature and joint-holdout RMSE.
With three cross-batch donors and validated links, control-adjusted batch-exclusive perturbations yielded coupling curvature 0.23 versus <0.01 unadjusted.
Match three cross-batch donors across batch-exclusive/bridging perturbations; contaminate control peaks with biological signal and measure coupling curvature and RMSE.
With 20% biological contamination in control peaks, batch-exclusive perturbations had coupling curvature <0.01; batch-bridging perturbations retained 0.18.
ControlPeakStress v1 records donor-matched exclusive/bridging perturbations, 0–20% control contamination, coupling curvature, and joint-holdout RMSE.
Allow batch-exclusive perturbations only with verified batch-only controls; require batch-bridging perturbations when controls carry biological signal.
Transport within-batch RNA perturbation contrasts using unpaired ATAC module scores, donor-overlap weighting, and placebo-batch falsification.
Do ATAC module scores predict perturbation-effect variation across donors, or merely encode batch structure after within-batch differencing?
With crossed donors and batch-overlapping perturbations, residual ATAC module scores explain donor-specific RNA contrasts beyond batch labels and placebo modules.
Evaluate donor-held-out RNA contrasts predicted from residual ATAC modules against batch labels and permuted placebo modules, stratifying perturbation overlap.
Using ControlPeakStress v1, predict held-out donor RNA contrasts from residual ATAC modules versus batch labels/placebos, stratified by perturbation overlap.
ControlPeakStress v1: crossed, bridging designs yielded donor-holdout contrast RMSE 0.67 with residual modules versus 0.81 batch-only and 0.80 placebo.
Benchmark overlap-weighted within-batch RNA-contrast transport using ATAC modules against RNA-only on joint donor–perturbation holdouts and placebo-batch permutations.
On crossed, bridging joint holdouts, ATAC-module transport RMSE was 0.78 versus RNA-only 0.80, missing the 15% improvement target.
Using ControlPeakStress v1, swap batch labels and permute donor-matched ATAC modules during transport; compare joint-holdout RMSE by control contamination.
With uncontaminated controls and three cross-batch donors, transport RMSE was 0.66 versus 0.80 RNA-only and 0.81 module-permuted.
Retain transport only with uncontaminated controls and three cross-batch donors; otherwise 0.78 RMSE fails the 15% target.
Train a partial-identification-gated RNA–ATAC ensemble, using ATAC only when donor overlap and negative-control bounds exclude batch-only explanations.
What coupling-bound width safely gates ATAC use under control-peak contamination while preserving ≥15% joint-holdout RMSE improvement?
Zero-excluding coupling bounds ≤0.20 wide yield gated joint-holdout RMSE ≤0.68 versus 0.80 RNA-only across 0–20% control contamination.
Sweep coupling-bound widths and control contamination in donor-overlap strata; assess gating decisions, bound coverage, and joint-holdout RMSE.
Using ControlPeakStress v1, sweep zero-excluding bound-width gates (0.10–0.30) across contamination and donor overlap; measure coverage and joint-holdout RMSE.
With three cross-batch donors, ≤0.20 gates achieved joint-holdout RMSE 0.68 versus 0.80 RNA-only across 0–20% control contamination.
Using ControlPeakStress v1, introduce perturbation-correlated contamination into control peaks; audit ≤0.20 gates for coupling-bound coverage and joint-holdout RMSE.
At 20% perturbation-correlated control contamination, ≤0.20 gates yielded joint-holdout RMSE 0.75 versus 0.80 RNA-only, missing 15% improvement.
A ≤0.20 zero-excluding bound gate achieves RMSE ≤0.68 only when controls pass perturbation-independence tests and three donors cross batches.
Screen controls with within-batch perturbation permutations, then test ≤0.20 gates on three-crossed-donor joint-holdout RMSE and bound coverage.
On ControlPeakStress v1, compare permutation-screened versus unscreened ≤0.20 gates across 0–20% perturbation-correlated contamination; record three-crossed-donor joint-holdout RMSE and coverage.
Among batch-bridging perturbations, three crossed donors with 20% correlated, independence-failing controls achieved gated RMSE 0.67 versus RNA-only 0.80.
Using ControlPeakStress v1, compare screened/unscreened ≤0.20 gates across perturbation overlap with 20% correlated contamination; measure three-donor RMSE.
At 20% contamination, batch-exclusive designs with three crossed donors yielded RMSE 0.67 with independence-passing controls versus 0.75 with failing controls.
GateAudit v1 tabulates control-independence results, perturbation overlap, coupling-bound widths, three-donor joint-holdout RMSE, and bound coverage.
Using GateAudit v1, stratify three-crossed-donor ≤0.20 gates by control independence and perturbation overlap; test joint-holdout RMSE ≤0.68 and bound coverage.
GateAudit v1: batch-exclusive gates with three crossed donors and independence-passing controls yielded 0.67 RMSE versus 0.80 RNA-only.
Deploy ≤0.20 gates with three crossed donors: require independence-passing controls for batch-exclusive perturbations, but allow batch-bridging despite failing controls.
Using GateAudit v1, test gated RNA–ATAC against RNA-only on PerturbTransfer-6 unseen-donor/perturbation holdouts; assess ≥15% RMSE improvement and nested-design identifiability.
PerturbTransfer-6: gated joint-holdout RMSE was 0.67 versus RNA-only 0.80 (16.3% lower) with three crossed donors; nested designs defaulted to RNA-only.
Do donor-by-batch interactions invalidate zero-excluding coupling bounds despite three crossed donors and batch-bridging perturbations?
Inject donor-by-batch accessibility interactions, then audit bound coverage, false ATAC gating, and joint-holdout RMSE across interaction strengths.
Extend GateAudit v1 with 0–30% donor-by-batch ATAC interactions; measure coupling-bound coverage, false gating, and joint-holdout RMSE in bridging designs.
At 25% donor-by-batch interaction, coupling-bound coverage fell to 72% and gated RMSE rose to 0.77 versus RNA-only 0.80.
Retain gated ATAC for additive-batch designs; fall back to RNA-only when donor-by-batch interactions threaten coupling-bound coverage.

Implement TransferGate v1 with rank/overlap, control-independence, perturbation-bridging, transport-eligibility, and interaction checks; benchmark joint-holdout RMSE and nonidentifiable-design fallbacks.
TransferGate v1 packages eligibility checks, RNA-only fallbacks, coupling-bound diagnostics, and joint donor–perturbation holdout RMSE reports.
